proposal: Add three missing tests to the test file of the first build of a command-line tool (Python 3.9, standard library only) that prints the lines, words and characters of standard input on one line, or only the words with the option --words. The tests check the output line and the --words option, each run through the tool's entry function, and exit status 2 when the input cannot be read. Each build of a tool is kept in its own folder; the newest is the one in work, and earlier builds stay as they were. As first submitted, the proposal also added an enforcer: a test that reads the tool's live specification and fails when a behaviour the specification names has no test named after it (the name lowercased, non-letters as _). It also added an edit to the specification that listed the output and 'input not valid UTF-8' as two more named behaviours.
feedback: The missing tests are right: output and --words through the entry function, and exit status 2 on unreadable input. The enforcer as designed is not. First, it breaks the rule that earlier builds stay as they were. The first build's test file would read the live specification. When the specification grows for the next build, the first build's tests start failing even though the first build has not changed. Second, its naming rule contradicts its own tests. '--words' lowercased with non-letters as _ gives test___words, not test_words_option. Third, the edit to the specification is not needed. Output is already stated in the specification's first sentence and example. Unreadable input is covered by a standard in the project's standards file, which already binds every tool. Copying it as 'not valid UTF-8' narrows 'cannot be read'. Recommend that the proposal's author resubmit with just the three tests and no edit to the specification. That part can be approved as it stands. The enforcer can be proposed separately once it reads the specification as of its own build. The author resubmitted as asked: the three tests, no edit to the specification, no enforcer, and a check of three mutants (deliberately broken copies of the tool), one failing each test. Approve.

corrections.field: upsides: named behaviours with a test
corrections.to: 3 to 5, counting the specification's four named behaviours plus the project's exit-status standard
corrections.reason: with no edit to the specification, output is the specification's sentence and example, not a sixth named behaviour; the count depends on the edit this review drops

pattern.context: A project keeps each build of a tool in its own folder, with its tests beside it, and earlier builds stay as they were. A proposal adds tests a build is missing, and bundles a guard that ties test names to the behaviours the specification names.
pattern.problem: The guard reads the live specification, so an old build's tests fail whenever the specification grows for a later build, though the old build has not changed. Its rule for turning a behaviour's name into a test name does not produce the names its own tests use. The bundled edit to the specification restates what the specification and the project's standards already say, and in restating narrows 'cannot be read' to 'not valid UTF-8'.
pattern.solution: Approve the missing tests alone, with no edit to the specification, and prove each with a mutant (a deliberately broken copy of the tool) that fails it. Leave the guard for a separate proposal in which it reads the specification as of its own build.
pattern.consequences: The build gains its three tests now, each shown to fail on a broken copy. Earlier builds keep passing as the specification grows. The count of named behaviours with a test is 3 to 5, not 3 to 6 of 6, because output stays a sentence and example rather than a named behaviour.
